---
title: "00 — Mathematical Foundations and Proof"
---

## Why this topic matters

A fast implementation solves the model you gave it. Mathematics helps you
decide whether that model describes the problem. This chapter develops the
habits behind a correct reduction: specifying objects, proving both directions,
counting each object once, and distinguishing evidence from a proof.

You already know algorithms and programming. No prior course in proofs or
algebra is required. If notation is familiar, use the exercises to locate gaps;
you do not need to pass a mathematical entrance examination.

## Prerequisites and learning objectives

Prerequisite: arithmetic with integers and fractions. The
[notation reference](../NOTATION.qmd) collects conventions used later.
After this chapter you should be able to translate a quantified claim,
choose an appropriate proof method, derive Bézout's identity, and justify a
counting formula or state invariant without relying on small-case evidence.

## Definitions and notation

The sets $\mathbb Z$, $\mathbb Q$, and $\mathbb R$ contain integers, rational
numbers (fractions of integers with nonzero denominator), and real numbers.
Write $\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ for nonnegative integers. A set has no repeated
elements; a sequence has order and may repeat. The empty set is $\varnothing$,
and $|S|$ is the number of elements of a finite set $S$.

The interval $[0,n)$ means the integers $0,\ldots,n-1$ when used for indices.
An indexed sum $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}a_i$ adds one term for each such index. An empty
sum is zero; an empty product is one. These conventions make recurrences work
at size zero: there is one empty sequence, even though it contains no elements.

A function $f:A\to B$ assigns one output in $B$ to each input in $A$.
It is *injective* if different inputs have different outputs, *surjective* if
every output is reached, and *bijective* if both hold. A bijection proves
$|A|=|B|$ for finite sets because it pairs their elements one for one.

An indicator $[P]$ is $1$ if a proposition $P$ is true and $0$ otherwise.
For example, $\sum_{i=1}^{10}[2\mid i]=5$ counts even integers in that range.
The symbol $a\mid b$ means $b=ak$ for some integer $k$; its negation is
$a\nmid b$. The floor $\lfloor x\rfloor$ is the greatest integer at most $x$,
so $\lfloor-3/2\rfloor=-2$, which differs from truncation toward zero.

## Logic: what exactly must be proved?

The statement $P\Rightarrow Q$ means every instance satisfying $P$ also
satisfies $Q$. Its converse $Q\Rightarrow P$ is a different claim.
The notation $P\Longleftrightarrow Q$ requires both directions. A reduction
claiming that feasible solutions correspond must prove both directions unless
it explicitly needs only a bound.

The quantifiers $\forall$ and $\exists$ mean “for every” and “there exists.”
Their order matters. For every integer $x$ there exists an integer $y>x$;
there does not exist one integer $y$ larger than every integer $x$.
To disprove a universal claim, one counterexample suffices. To negate
“for every $x$ there exists $y$ with $P(x,y)$,” say “there exists $x$ for
which every $y$ fails $P(x,y)$.”

**Worked failure: an invalid converse.** If a positive integer is divisible by
$6$, it is divisible by $3$. The reverse implication fails at $3$.
Thus checking a necessary condition can reject impossible instances, but
passing it does not construct a solution.

For implication proofs, the *contrapositive* $\neg Q\Rightarrow\neg P$ is
equivalent to $P\Rightarrow Q$. For example, to prove that $n^2$ even forces
$n$ even, take odd $n=2k+1$. Then
$n^2=2(2k^2+2k)+1$ is odd. A proof by contradiction instead assumes the
claim is false and derives an impossibility.

## Induction: a recurrence for correctness

To prove $P(n)$ for all integers $n\ge n_0$, prove the base $P(n_0)$ and
prove $P(n)\Rightarrow P(n+1)$. The base starts a chain that reaches every
allowed index. In strong induction, the step may use all smaller valid indices.
Both are natural for dynamic programming: the mathematical dependency graph
must reach already proved states.

**Worked example: a sum.** Let $S_n=1+\cdots+n$, with $S_0=0$.
We claim $S_n=n(n+1)/2$. It holds at $0$. Assuming it at $n$,

$$S_{n+1}=S_n+(n+1)
=\frac{n(n+1)}2+(n+1)
=\frac{(n+1)(n+2)}2.$$

Each equality uses the definition, the induction hypothesis, or ordinary
algebra. This proof is over the integers/rationals. When computing modulo
$m$, divide the even integer factor by $2$ before reduction; $2$ need not
have an inverse modulo $m$.

**Worked example: prime factorization exists.** A prime is an integer $p\ge2$
whose only positive divisors are $1,p$. By strong induction, every $n\ge2$
is a product of primes. If $n$ is prime, we are done. Otherwise $n=ab$ with
$2\le a,b<n$, so the induction hypotheses factor both $a$ and $b$.
This proves existence, not yet uniqueness; uniqueness follows below.

**Failed induction.** “All objects in every set have the same color” has a true
one-element base. Comparing the first $n$ and last $n$ elements of an
$(n+1)$-element set would transfer color through their overlap only when
$n\ge2$. The step from one to two has empty overlap. An induction step must
work at the first boundary, not only for large indices.

## Invariants, potential functions, and extremal choice

An *invariant* is a property preserved by every allowed transition. Prove it
initially and after one arbitrary transition. A *potential function* assigns
a value to a state that moves in a controlled direction. A nonnegative integer
potential that strictly decreases proves termination; a real-valued decrease
alone need not, as $1,1/2,1/4,\ldots$ illustrates.

**Worked impossibility and construction.** On a binary board, one move flips
exactly two cells. The parity of the number of ones is invariant: a move
changes it by $-2,0,$ or $2$. Hence a board with one one cannot become all zero.
Even parity is only a necessary condition until the allowed pairs are specified.
If the allowed-pair graph is connected, it is also sufficient: take a spanning
tree, process leaves upward, and flip a leaf with its parent exactly when
the leaf is one. Cleared leaves never change again. The root is finally zero
because total parity is even. This gives an $O(V+E)$ construction using a
graph traversal, where $V$ counts cells and $E$ allowed pairs.

An *extremal argument* selects a smallest, largest, or otherwise optimal object
and exploits what it cannot do. Every finite nonempty set of integers has a
minimum. Every nonempty set of nonnegative integers has a minimum even if infinite.

**Worked example: a tree has a leaf.** In a finite tree with at least two
vertices, take a longest simple path. An endpoint cannot have another neighbor:
a neighbor off the path extends it, while a neighbor elsewhere on the path
creates a cycle. Thus each endpoint has degree one. This is why repeatedly
removing leaves supports induction in the matrix-tree theorem.

## Euclid and Bézout: deriving a central algebraic tool

For nonnegative $a,b$, not both zero, their greatest common divisor
$g=\gcd(a,b)$ is the greatest positive integer dividing both. Division with
remainder gives $a=qb+r$ with $0\le r<b$ when $b>0$.
A number divides both $a,b$ exactly when it divides both $b,r=a-qb$.
Therefore $\gcd(a,b)=\gcd(b,r)$. The positive remainders decrease, so
Euclid's algorithm terminates, and its last nonzero remainder is $g$.

Every remainder is an integer linear combination of $a,b$: the starting
values are, and subtracting $q$ times one combination from another preserves
that property. Consequently there exist integers $u,v$ such that

$$au+bv=g.$$

This is *Bézout's identity*. For $a=30,b=18$, the remainders are $12,6,0$,
and back substitution gives $6=18-(30-18)=2\cdot18-30$.
It follows that $30x+18y=6$ has $(x,y)=(-1,2)$ as one solution.

For arbitrary integer $c$, the equation $ax+by=c$ has integer solutions iff
$g\mid c$. Necessity holds because $g$ divides every left side; sufficiency
comes from multiplying Bézout's coefficients by $c/g$.
When $a,b>0$, all solutions from one $(x_0,y_0)$ are

$$x=x_0+\frac bg t,\qquad y=y_0-\frac ag t,\qquad t\in\mathbb Z.$$

To prove completeness, subtract two solutions: $(a/g)\Delta x=-(b/g)\Delta y$.
The coefficients $a/g,b/g$ are coprime. Bézout then implies $b/g\mid\Delta x$,
which forces exactly the parameterization above. Zero coefficients are handled
directly; if both coefficients are zero, solvability is exactly $c=0$.

Euclid uses $O(\log\max(a,b))$ integer divisions for positive inputs:
in two remainder steps the larger argument at least halves. This counts
arithmetic operations; large-integer division has its own bit cost.

**Why prime factorization is unique.** If prime $p$ divides $ab$ but not $a$,
then $\gcd(p,a)=1$. Multiply a Bézout equation for $p,a$ by $b$ to conclude
$p\mid b$. Thus a prime appearing in one factorization must appear in any
other factorization of the same integer. Cancel that prime and repeat.
This proves uniqueness up to the order of the factors.

## Double counting and bijections

Before rearranging a sum, name the objects represented by its terms.
In a finite undirected graph, count incidences $(v,e)$ where vertex $v$ is an
endpoint of edge $e$. Summing by vertex gives $\sum_v\deg(v)$; summing by
edge gives $2|E|$. Thus the two expressions agree. Here edges have two distinct
endpoints; with loops, define degree by endpoint occurrences instead.

For subsets, let $\binom nk$ count $k$-element subsets of an $n$-element set;
it is zero when $k<0$ or $k>n$. Count ordered lists of $k$ distinct elements:
there are $n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$. Each subset has exactly $k!$ orderings, so

$$\binom nk=\frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!},\qquad 0\le k\le n.$$

The quotient is exact in the integers. The factorial $n!$ is the product of
$1,\ldots,n$, with $0!=1$. Choosing whether a distinguished element is present
also gives $\binom nk=\binom{n-1}k+\binom{n-1}{k-1}$ for $n\ge1$.

**Worked example: choose a team and captain.** From $n\ge1$ people choose a
nonempty subset and distinguish one member. Choosing size first gives
$\sum_{k=1}^n k\binom nk$. Choosing the captain first gives $n$ choices,
then every other person independently joins or does not: $2^{n-1}$ choices.
Therefore $\sum_k k\binom nk=n2^{n-1}$. For $n=3$, $3+6+3=12=3\cdot4$.
The power of two counts subsets, not permutations.

## Contest translation and checklist

Use a library routine only after the reduction has an input/output contract.
Keep four statements separate: the model is correct, every solution is
represented, the algorithm finds the required result, and the resource bound
fits the constraints. Exhaustive tests can refute any of these claims on a
small case; passing tests does not replace the proof for arbitrary inputs.

- What is the domain, including empty and zero cases?
- Is the proposed condition necessary, sufficient, or both?
- Which object does one summand or DP state represent?
- What is preserved by a transition, and what ensures termination?
- Are counted fibers all the same size before dividing?
- Does the complexity count arithmetic operations or actual machine work?

## Exercises, hints, and solutions

### 1. Quantifiers and a counterexample — concept check

Negate “every pair of nonzero residues modulo $m$ has a nonzero product.”
Find the smallest $m\ge2$ where the original claim fails.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint and solution"}
Seek two nonzero factors of the modulus. The negation says that there exist
two nonzero residues whose product is zero. Modulo $4$, $2\cdot2=0$; modulo
$2$ and $3$, direct multiplication shows no such pair. The answer is $4$.
This is the first warning that a nonzero element need not be invertible.
:::

### 2. Count the same marked subset twice — derivation

For $n\ge2$, derive $\sum_{k=0}^n k(k-1)\binom nk=n(n-1)2^{n-2}$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint and solution"}
Mark an ordered pair of distinct members in the chosen subset. For a
$k$-element subset there are $k(k-1)$ such pairs. Alternatively choose the
ordered marked pair first in $n(n-1)$ ways, then choose any of the remaining
$n-2$ elements. Both counts describe exactly the same objects. For $n=3$,
the left side is $2\cdot3+6\cdot1=12$.
:::

### 3. All bounded solutions — modelling

Find all nonnegative integer pairs satisfying $6x+9y=45$ and $x\le6$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint and solution"}
Divide by $3$. The equation $2x+3y=15$ has one solution $(0,5)$.
Every solution is $x=3t,y=5-2t$. Bounds imply $0\le t\le2$.
The pairs are $(0,5),(3,3),(6,1)$. Guessing one solution would miss two;
the parameterization proves completeness.
:::

### 4. Flip graph — synthesis

Extend the two-cell flip model to a graph that may be disconnected. Give a
necessary and sufficient condition for reaching all zero and a construction.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint and solution"}
Each move stays inside one connected component, so parity in every component
is invariant. Even parity in each component is sufficient by the spanning-tree
leaf procedure applied independently. An isolated vertex must already be zero.
Components plus the construction cost $O(V+E)$, with at most $V-1$ tree-edge
flips overall when the graph is nonempty. This proof combines an obstruction
with a construction, which is stronger than either alone.
:::

## Summary and reference sheet

An implication needs one direction; an equivalence needs two. Induction needs
a valid base and a step at every boundary. An invariant proves preservation;
a decreasing nonnegative integer potential proves termination. A bijection or
double count proves equality by describing the same finite objects twice.

For integers $a,b$ not both zero, Bézout gives $au+bv=\gcd(a,b)$.
Thus $ax+by=c$ is solvable exactly when the gcd divides $c$.
Binomial coefficients count unordered subsets; factorial division is exact
over integers and needs separate justification modulo a modulus.

Continue with [modular algebra](../01-modular-algebra/chapter.qmd). Later,
[combinatorics](../04-combinatorics/chapter.qmd),
[linear algebra](../10-linear-algebra/chapter.qmd), and
[probability](../11-probability/chapter.qmd) develop the other former
entrance diagnostics from their mathematical definitions.
